nameStory: The Channeled Barrel-bubble gets its name from its distinctive shape and surface features. Like a tiny barrel, this sea snail has a rounded, cylindrical shell, while the 'channeled' part refers to the grooved lines that spiral around its surface. The 'bubble' portion comes from the translucent, delicate quality of its thin shell that can look almost soap-bubble fragile.
description: The Channeled Barrel-bubble is a small marine snail that lives in New England's coastal waters. This gastropod mollusk has a smooth, cylindrical shell that's typically whitish or pale in color. It belongs to a group called bubble snails, which are known for their thin, often translucent shells. These little sea creatures are carnivorous, feeding on other small marine organisms.

idTips.label: Shell shape
idTips.description: Cylindrical and barrel-like with a rounded body whorl that makes up most of the shell's length, feeling smooth and lightweight when handled

idTips.label: Spiral channels
idTips.description: Fine grooved lines or channels that spiral around the shell surface, visible when viewed closely and feelable with a gentle touch

idTips.label: Shell color
idTips.description: Typically whitish, cream, or pale yellow with a somewhat translucent quality that allows light to pass through the thin shell walls

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Small enough to fit comfortably on a fingertip, usually less than half an inch in length

idTips.label: Shell opening
idTips.description: Narrow aperture (opening) that extends nearly the full length of the shell, with smooth edges

habitat: Look for Channeled Barrel-bubbles in sandy or muddy bottoms of shallow coastal waters along New England's shoreline. They prefer areas with soft sediments where they can burrow and hunt for prey. You might find empty shells washed up on beaches after storms, particularly in areas with gentle wave action.

seasonality.spring: Active in warming waters as plankton blooms provide food for their larvae. Empty shells may begin washing ashore more frequently.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most likely to be found in shallow waters. Best time to spot live specimens in tide pools or shallow sandy areas.
seasonality.fall: Still active but may move to slightly deeper waters. Fresh shells continue to wash up on beaches during autumn storms.
seasonality.winter: Less active in cold waters, typically found in deeper areas. Beach-combing after winter storms may yield well-preserved shells.

funFact: Despite being called a 'bubble snail,' the Channeled Barrel-bubble is actually a fierce predator that can extend its body far outside its shell to engulf prey that's sometimes larger than the shell itself!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other small, pale shells on the beach, but the distinctive barrel shape and spiral channels set it apart from more common periwinkles or moon snail shells, which are either more conical or completely round.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'bubble snail' might be misleading since these aren't the fragile, soap-bubble-like creatures the name suggests, but rather sturdy predatory snails with relatively thin but durable shells adapted for life in sandy sediments.
compareHints: Since this is the only Acteocina species commonly found in New England waters, compare it with other bubble snails in the Tornatinidae family, which tend to have more elongated or ovate shells rather than the distinctly barrel-like shape. Other bubble snails also typically lack the prominent channeled grooves that give this species its diagnostic spiral-lined appearance.
